text: The List of Azerbaijani Heroes of the Soviet Union lists all ethnic Azerbaijani Heroes of the Soviet Union, along with their unit and rank at the time of action and the date of the award.
The title Hero of the Soviet Union was the highest distinction of the Soviet Union, and 42 Azerbaijanis were awarded it, including three whose ethnicity is disputed.
All Azerbaijani Heroes of the Soviet Union received their award for actions in World War II, and Hazi Aslanov was the only Azerbaijani to receive the title twice.
Bahatdin Shahveled oglu Mirzayev (31 December 1914 to 15 April 1987) was an Azerbaijani Red Army captain and a Hero of the Soviet Union.

During World War II, Bahatdin Shahveled oglu Mirzayev served as a battery commander in the 416th Rifle Division, and during the Vistula-Oder Offensive he corrected his battery's fire, was wounded, and reportedly enabled the battery to destroy multiple German firing points.

During the Vistula-Oder Offensive, the battery commanded by Bahatdin Shahveled oglu Mirzayev knocked out German artillery pieces that were slowing the infantry's advance on the day after he was wounded, and two days after the offensive began it destroyed two German tanks and an armored personnel carrier, enabling the capture of the village.
Bahatdin Shahveled oglu Mirzayev received the title Hero of the Soviet Union on 24 March 1945, was seriously wounded in the Battle of Berlin, and was discharged upon recovery.
Postwar, Bahatdin Shahveled oglu Mirzayev worked as head of the militarized guard department at the Azerbaijan SSR Ministry of Communications.
Georgy Vasilyevich Ivanov (25 May 1901 to 25 December 2001) was a Soviet Army major general and Hero of the Soviet Union.
Georgy Vasilyevich Ivanov was awarded the title Hero of the Soviet Union and the Order of Lenin for his leadership of the 6th Guards Rifle Division from late 1944 to 1945.
Georgy Vasilyevich Ivanov fought in World War II at the Battle of the Dnieper and the Vistula-Oder Offensive.
Mike Gundy (born August 12, 1967) is an American football coach and former player who is currently the head football coach at Oklahoma State University.
Mike Gundy played college football at Oklahoma State, where he played quarterback from 1986 to 1989, and he became Oklahoma State's coach on January 3, 2005.
In 2007, Mike Gundy received national media attention for his heated criticism of a newspaper article on one of his players.
Karl Brill was an American football player who played at the tackle position for the Harvard Crimson football team in 1904 and 1905 and was selected as a first-team All-American in 1905.

As a sophomore in December 1905, Karl Brill announced that he would not continue playing football, saying he came to Harvard to get a degree as a mining engineer and that varsity football had played havoc with his studies.

Karl Brill also denounced football on moral grounds, stating that the human body was not meant to withstand the strain football demands and calling the game a mere gladiatorial combat that is brutal throughout.
Mariam Stepanyan (born 22 September 1989) is an Armenian professional footballer who currently plays for the Armenia women's national football team.
Before starting football, Mariam Stepanyan was a player of the Armenian National Women's Team of Handball, and she began playing football in 2007 with FC Banants.
Mariam Stepanyan was twice Armenian league champion with FC Banants, and after that she was twice Armenian champion with Yerevan FC G.M. and received the best defenders title of the season.
Frank John Mahoney Jr. (October 25, 1901 to November 21, 1961) was an American football back who played five seasons with the Chicago Cardinals of the National Football League.

Frank John Mahoney Jr. played college football at Creighton University, attended the Omaha High School of Commerce in Omaha, Nebraska, and was a member of the Chicago Cardinals team that were NFL champions in 1925.

Frank John Mahoney Jr. also played baseball, basketball and track and field, and played for the Chicago Bruins of the American Basketball League; he had received an offer to play baseball for the Pittsburgh Pirates but opted to play football for the Chicago Cardinals.
Robert Bruce 'Bob' Adams (born August 15, 1946) is a former professional American football tight end in the National Football League and a spokesperson for the Church of Scientology International.

Bob Adams attended El Camino High School during the 1960s and was encouraged by a coach at the College of San Mateo to play football, playing a single season there in 1966 while also participating in track-and-field and basketball.

Doug Scovil, a former coach of the College of San Mateo, recruited Bob Adams to the College of the Pacific, where Bob Adams received a full scholarship to play football, and by 1968 Bob Adams was captain of the team's offense.

Indoor soccer, or arena soccer, is a game derived from association football adapted for play in a walled indoor arena, and it is known internationally as indoor football, minifootball, fast football, floorball or showball.

Indoor soccer, as it is most often known in the United States and Canada, was originally developed in those two countries as a way to play football during the winter months, when snow would make outdoor play difficult.

In the United States and Canada, areas such as hockey rinks or basketball courts are adapted for indoor soccer play, while in Mexico the game is called fast football (futbol rapido), in South America showbol, and in Spain indoor football (futbol indoor).

Wesley Theodore 'Moose' Englehorn (January 21, 1890 to September 3, 1993) was an American football player and coach born in Helena, Montana, who died at age 103, and before his death he lived at Stapeley Hall, a home for the elderly in the Germantown section of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, and was the oldest living All-American football player.

Wesley Theodore 'Moose' Englehorn first gained fame as a football player for Spokane High School, and in 1907 a newspaper reported that he was expected to enter an eastern college, after Princeton University had reportedly recruited him, though he did not enroll at Princeton and instead played for two years on the All Star Pacific Northwest football and basketball teams.

Wesley Theodore 'Moose' Englehorn played one year of football at Washington State College before enrolling at Dartmouth College, where he played two years at the tackle position and was selected as a first-team All-American in 1912.

Wesley Theodore 'Moose' Englehorn was elected Dartmouth team captain for the 1913 season but was declared ineligible under the so-called three-year rule because of his year at Washington State, so he served as the team's assistant coach that year and was elected class president.

After graduating from Dartmouth in 1914, Wesley Theodore 'Moose' Englehorn coached Case School of Applied Science in Cleveland, Ohio from 1914 to 1916, was line coach at Colgate University in 1917, assisted Frank Cavanaugh at Boston College in 1920, and was Amherst College's head football coach in 1921 before announcing his retirement from coaching in January 1922.
Joseph Cale Gundy (born April 10, 1972) is a former American football quarterback who played for the Oklahoma Sooners from 1990 to 1993.
While at Oklahoma, Joseph Cale Gundy was a member of the Delta Tau Delta International Fraternity.
After coaching running backs for 16 years at Oklahoma, Joseph Cale Gundy was promoted to Assistant Head Coach and moved to Inside Receivers for the 2015 season.
Joseph Cale Gundy's brother is Mike Gundy, who is the head football coach at Oklahoma State University.
Ben Terrence Coates (born August 16, 1969) is a former American football tight end in the National Football League, a former CIAA football coach, and a former NFL tight ends coach.
Ben Terrence Coates did not play football until his senior year at Greenwood High School, and was a multi-sport player at Livingstone College located in Salisbury, North Carolina.

As a gridiron player at Livingstone College, Ben Terrence Coates broke nearly all meaningful records at the school, but because his split-sport performances came against weak competition for a non-notable school, he received little notice outside the CIAA.
While a college student at Livingstone College, Ben Terrence Coates joined the Phi Beta Sigma fraternity through the Upsilon Chapter at the school.
Chris Rubio is an American trainer of long snappers in American football who works with high school long snappers and evaluates them for college football programs.
The Rubio's Long Snapping camp run by Chris Rubio is the longest running in the nation, and over the past 12 years Chris Rubio has helped over 500 long snappers play football in college and the NFL.
Chris Rubio partners with Chris Sailer, who provides a similar service for placekickers and punters through Chris Sailer Kicking, and the two were teammates in college with the UCLA Bruins.

The Truth is the debut studio album of American country music singer Brady Seals and his first solo album after leaving the country band Little Texas, and it was released on February 25, 1997 on Reprise Records.
The Truth includes the singles 'Another You, Another Me', 'Still Standing Tall', and 'Natural Born Lovers', and of these only 'Another You, Another Me' reached the Top 40 on Hot Country Songs.
Brady Seals co-wrote all but two of the songs on The Truth and co-produced the album with Rodney Crowell.
Nick Carter, Master Detective was a Mutual radio crime drama based on tales of the fictional private detective Nick Carter from Street & Smith's dime novels and pulp magazines.
Nick Carter first came to radio as The Return of Nick Carter, a reference to the character's pulp origins, but the title was soon changed to Nick Carter, Master Detective.
A veteran radio dramatist, Ferrin Fraser, wrote many of the scripts for Nick Carter, Master Detective.
'Another You, Another Me' is a debut solo song recorded by American country music artist Brady Seals, released in September 1996 as the first single from the album The Truth.
'Another You, Another Me' reached number 32 on the Billboard Hot Country Singles & Tracks chart.
'Another You, Another Me' was written by Brady Seals's uncle, Troy Seals, along with Will Jennings.

Brady Seals (born March 29, 1969) is an American country music artist who is the cousin of Jim Seals of Seals & Crofts, Dan Seals and Johnny Duncan, the nephew of Troy Seals, and the husband of former BNA Records recording artist Lisa Stewart.
Brady Seals made his debut in 1988 as co-lead vocalist and keyboardist in the sextet Little Texas, with whom he recorded until his departure in late 1994.
Between leaving Little Texas and 2002, Brady Seals recorded as a solo singer, releasing three studio albums and charting in the Top 40 on the country charts with 'Another You, Another Me'.

In 2002, Brady Seals formed a quartet called Hot Apple Pie, in which he has recorded one studio album and charted three singles, and his fourth solo album, 'Play Time', was released in 2009 via Star City.
Nick Carter va tout casser is a French action film starring Eddie Constantine as Nick Carter, and it was titled License to Kill in the USA.
An English version of Nick Carter va tout casser was dubbed by Eddie Constantine, who dubbed himself.
Eddie Constantine repeated his role as Nick Carter in the 1965 French action film Nick Carter et le trèfle rouge.
Nickolas Gene 'Nick' Carter (born January 28, 1980) is an American singer, songwriter, actor, and dancer who is best known as a member of the pop group the Backstreet Boys.

As of 2015, Nick Carter had released three solo albums, 'Now or Never', 'I'm Taking Off' and 'All American', during breaks between Backstreet Boys schedules, and a collaboration with Jordan Knight titled 'Nick & Knight'.

Nick Carter has made occasional television appearances and starred in his own reality shows, 'House of Carters' and 'I (Heart) Nick Carter', and he gained fame in the mid 1990s and early 2000s as a teen idol.
Nick Carter, the Backstreet Boys singer, is the older brother of singer Aaron Carter and the late Leslie Carter.
'My Love' is a song recorded by the American country music band Little Texas and was released in January 1994 as the third single from the album Big Time.
'My Love' was co-written by Little Texas keyboardist Brady Seals, who also sang lead vocals on it, lead guitarist Porter Howell, and Tommy Barnes.
'My Love' reached the top of the Billboard country singles charts, becoming Little Texas's only Number One country hit.
Brady Seals is the self-titled second album by American country music singer Brady Seals, and it is his second release independently of the band Little Texas, of which he was a member until 1995.
The self-titled Brady Seals album includes the singles 'I Fell', 'Whole Lotta Hurt' and 'The Best Is Yet to Come'.
All three singles from Brady Seals's self-titled second album charted on the Billboard country charts, although all three missed the Top 40.
Nick Carter et le trèfle rouge (Nick Carter and Red Club) is a 1965 French action film that features the successful literary character Nick Carter and is based on a novel by Claude Rank.
Nick Carter et le trèfle rouge is a sequel to the 1964 French action film Nick Carter va tout casser.
Thompson Street is the third solo album by American country music singer Brady Seals, released in February 2003 via Image Entertainment.
No singles were released from Thompson Street, and after its release Brady Seals founded the band Hot Apple Pie.

The Hassan II Mosque, also called the Grande Mosquée Hassan II and colloquially the 'Casablanca Hajj', is a mosque in Casablanca, Morocco, and it is the largest mosque in Morocco and the 13th largest in the world.
The minaret of the Hassan II Mosque is the world's tallest at 210 m and is 60 stories high, topped by a laser whose light is directed towards Mecca.

The Hassan II Mosque was completed in 1993, designed by Michel Pinseau and built by Bouygues, and it stands on a promontory looking out to the Atlantic Ocean, with hand-crafted marble walls and a retractable roof, though there is no glass floor looking into the sea.
A maximum of 105,000 worshippers can gather at the Hassan II Mosque, with 25,000 inside the mosque hall and another 80,000 on the mosque's outside grounds.

Nusretiye Mosque is an ornate mosque located in the Tophane district of Beyoğlu, Istanbul, Turkey, whose architecture is influenced by Islamic elements while retaining a Baroque style that makes it unique to the city.
Nusretiye Mosque was built in 1823-1826 by Sultan Mahmut II, making it a Baroque-influenced mosque of the early nineteenth century in Istanbul.
The Gazi Atik Ali Pasha Mosque is an old Ottoman mosque located in the Çemberlitaş neighbourhood of the Fatih district in Istanbul, Turkey.
Construction of the Gazi Atik Ali Pasha Mosque was started under the orders of the future Grand Vizier Hadım Atik Ali Pasha in 1496 and was completed in 1497, during the reign of Sultan Bayezid II.
The Gazi Atik Ali Pasha Mosque is located near the entrance to the Kapalıçarşı (Grand Bazaar), the Column of Constantine, and the historical Nuruosmaniye Mosque.

The Vasat Atik Ali Pasha Mosque, also known as Zincirlikuyu Mosque or Karagümrük Mosque, is an Ottoman mosque located in the Karagümrük neighbourhood of the Fatih district in Istanbul, Turkey, on Fevzipaşa Street.

Sultan Bayezid II's grand vizier Hadım Atik Ali Pasha, after whom the Vasat Atik Ali Pasha Mosque is named, ordered its construction in 1502, and it was completed in 1512, one year after the grand vizier's death.
Bayezid II Mosque (Amasya) is a historical 15th century mosque in Amasya, Turkey, built in 1486 by order of the Ottoman sultan Bayezid II.
The Bayezid II Mosque in Amasya is the largest Külliye of the city of Amasya, Turkey.
The Yıldız Hamidiye Mosque, also called the Yıldız Mosque, is an Ottoman imperial mosque located in the Yıldız neighbourhood of the Beşiktaş district in Istanbul, Turkey, on the way to Yıldız Palace.
The Yıldız Hamidiye Mosque was commissioned by the Ottoman sultan Abdul Hamid II and constructed between 1884 and 1886, built on a rectangular plan with one minaret.

The architecture of the Yıldız Hamidiye Mosque combines Neo-Gothic style with classical Ottoman motifs, and a bronze colonnade erected by Abdul Hamid II in Marjeh Square of Damascus, Syria bears a replica statue of the Yıldız Mosque on top.
The King Mosque (Albanian: Xhamia e Mbretit), also known as the Sultan's Mosque or Sultan Bayezid Mosque, is a mosque and a Cultural Monument of Albania located in Berat.
The King Mosque in Berat was built in the 15th century by the Ottoman sultan Bayezid II for the local Albanian population, and it became a Cultural Monument in 1948.
The Bayezid II Mosque (Turkish: Beyazıt Camii, Bayezid Camii) is an Ottoman imperial mosque located in the Beyazıt Square area of Istanbul, Turkey.
The Bayezid II Mosque in Istanbul stands near the ruins of the Forum of Theodosius of ancient Constantinople.

Beyazıt Square (Turkish: Beyazıt Meydanı) is a square in the district of Fatih, in the European part of Istanbul, Turkey, officially named Freedom Square (Hürriyet Meydanı) but known as Beyazıt Square after the Bayezid II Mosque on one side of it.
Beyazıt Square is the former site of the Forum of Theodosius built by Constantine the Great, and its current form was designed by Turgut Cansever.
On one side of Beyazıt Square is the main entrance of Istanbul University, and the Beyazıt Tower, which is on the university's campus, can be seen from the square.

Nusretiye Clock Tower, also called Tophane Clock Tower, is a clock tower situated in Tophane, a neighborhood in Beyoğlu district of Istanbul, Turkey, next to Nusretiye Mosque and Tophane Kiosk at the European waterfront of the Bosphorus.
The Nusretiye Clock Tower was ordered by the Ottoman sultan Abdülmecid I (1823-1861), designed by architect Garabet Amira Balyan, and completed in 1848.
Three-peat is a term used primarily in American sports to refer to winning three consecutive championships, and it is a portmanteau of the words 'three' and 'repeat'.

The term three-peat originated with the Los Angeles Lakers of the National Basketball Association during their unsuccessful campaign for a third consecutive championship in the 1988-89 season, after they had won the previous two NBA Finals, in 1987 and 1988, against the Boston Celtics and Detroit Pistons.
The Lakers were swept by the Detroit Pistons in the 1989 NBA Finals, ending their bid for a third consecutive championship.

Three-peat is a registered trademark owned by Pat Riley, the Lakers' head coach from 1981-1990, although it was coined by L.A. player Byron Scott immediately after the Lakers' championship defense against the Detroit Pistons in the 1988 NBA Finals.
Chauncey Ray Billups (born September 25, 1976) is an American retired professional basketball player who played 17 seasons in the National Basketball Association.
Chauncey Ray Billups, a star at the University of Colorado, was selected third overall in the 1997 NBA draft by the Boston Celtics.

A five-time NBA All-Star and three-time All-NBA selection, Chauncey Ray Billups played for the Celtics, Toronto Raptors, Denver Nuggets, Minnesota Timberwolves, Detroit Pistons, New York Knicks, and Los Angeles Clippers during his NBA career.

Chauncey Ray Billups won the NBA Finals MVP in 2004 after helping the Pistons beat the Los Angeles Lakers, was nicknamed 'Mr. Big Shot' for making late-game shots with Detroit, and the Pistons retired his number #1 jersey in 2016.

Rickey Paulding (born October 23, 1982) is an American professional basketball player who played college basketball for the University of Missouri, scoring 1,200 points and grabbing 300 rebounds in his collegiate career.

Rickey Paulding scored 37 points and made nine threes against Dwyane Wade, Travis Diener and the Marquette Golden Eagles in the Tigers' loss in the 2nd round of the NCAA tournament in his junior year, and he then opted to return for his senior season.

Rickey Paulding was drafted 54th overall in the second round by the Detroit Pistons, and in his first year of pro ball he played for Hapoel Jerusalem of Israel after averaging 12.2 points per game for the Pistons in the summer leagues.
The Pistons waived Rickey Paulding the following year, and Rickey Paulding then tried out for the Sacramento Kings but failed to make the roster.
Rickey Paulding has played for Lyon Villeurbanne in France and BCM Gravelines Dunkerque Grand Littoral, and for the 2007/08 season signed with the German Bundesliga team EWE Baskets Oldenburg.
Reginald 'Reggie' Harding (May 4, 1942 to September 2, 1972) was an American professional basketball player who was drafted in 1962 by the Detroit Pistons.
Reggie Harding is noted as the first player drafted into the NBA without having played in college.

Reggie Harding spent five years in the NBA, playing for the Detroit Pistons, Chicago Bulls and later the Indiana Pacers, and also played for the Trenton Colonials of the Continental Basketball Association.

Jerome Williams (born May 10, 1973) is an American retired professional basketball player who last played for the New York Knicks of the NBA, and was a star player on the Magruder High School basketball team.

Jerome Williams was drafted out of Georgetown University by the Detroit Pistons with the 26th pick of the 1996 NBA Draft, a pick originally belonging to the San Antonio Spurs that went to the Pistons in the Dennis Rodman trade.
Jerome Williams played four-plus years with the Pistons, becoming one of their key reserves, and was a fan favorite during his days with the Toronto Raptors due to his tenacious efforts on the court.

The Detroit Pistons are an American professional basketball team based in Detroit, Michigan, that competes in the National Basketball Association as a member club of the league's Eastern Conference Central Division, and plays its home games at Little Caesars Arena.

The Detroit Pistons were founded in Fort Wayne, Indiana as the Fort Wayne (Zollner) Pistons in 1941, a member of the National Basketball League (NBL), and joined the Basketball Association of America (BAA) in 1948.
In 1949 the NBL and BAA merged to become the NBA, and since moving to Detroit in 1957 the Detroit Pistons have won three NBA championships, in 1989, 1990 and 2004.
The 2005-06 Detroit Pistons season was the 65th season of the franchise, the 58th in the National Basketball Association (NBA), and the 49th in the Detroit area.

The 2005-06 Detroit Pistons began the season hoping to improve upon their 54-28 output from the previous season, and they finished 64-18, their best record in franchise history, qualifying for the playoffs for the fifth straight season.

In the 2005-06 playoffs, the Detroit Pistons defeated the Milwaukee Bucks in five games in the first round and the Cleveland Cavaliers in a seven game series, reaching the Eastern Conference Finals for the fourth consecutive year before losing to the eventual NBA champions Miami Heat.
Ben Wallace, the Detroit Pistons' star defensive player, departed the team after the 2005-06 season on a free-agent deal with the Chicago Bulls.

Dennis Keith Rodman (born May 13, 1961) is an American retired professional basketball player who played for the Detroit Pistons, San Antonio Spurs, Chicago Bulls, Los Angeles Lakers, and Dallas Mavericks in the National Basketball Association.
Dennis Keith Rodman was nicknamed 'The Worm' and was known for his fierce defensive and rebounding abilities.
Gregory Keith Monroe Jr. (born June 4, 1990) is an American professional basketball player for the Milwaukee Bucks of the National Basketball Association.
In his freshman season at Georgetown University, Gregory Keith Monroe Jr. was named Big East Rookie of the Year.

Gregory Keith Monroe Jr. was drafted by the Detroit Pistons in the 2010 NBA draft with the seventh overall pick and became the last Pistons player to wear the #10 jersey, which the Pistons retired for Dennis Rodman at halftime of a game against the Chicago Bulls on April 1, 2011.
Prithipal Singh (28 January 1932 to 20 May 1983) was an Indian field hockey player nicknamed the 'King of short corner' by hockey commentators.
Prithipal Singh participated in the Olympic field hockey three times, and each time he scored the highest number of goals as a single player.
Prithipal Singh won Olympic medals at Rome in 1960 (silver), Tokyo in 1964 (gold) and Mexico in 1968 (bronze).
The first-ever Arjuna Award to a hockey player was conferred upon Prithipal Singh in 1961, and it was later followed by the Padma Shri in 1967.
The Evening Post, New Zealand commented in 1961 that to face the fury of Prithipal Singh's hit is to risk one's life.
The Yeni Valide Mosque (Turkish: Yeni Valide Camii) is an 18th-century Ottoman mosque in the Üsküdar district of Istanbul, Turkey.
The name Yeni Valide Mosque translates from Turkish as New Valide Mosque, and the Yeni Valide Mosque dates from the 18th century.
The Yeni Cami, meaning New Mosque, was originally named the Valide Sultan Mosque and later the New Valide Sultan Mosque after its partial reconstruction and completion between 1660 and 1665.

The Yeni Cami is an Ottoman imperial mosque located in the Eminönü quarter of Istanbul, Turkey, on the Golden Horn at the southern end of the Galata Bridge, and it is one of the famous architectural landmarks of Istanbul.
The Gazi Atik Ali Pasha Mosque is an old Ottoman mosque located in the Çemberlitaş neighbourhood of the Fatih district in Istanbul, Turkey.
Construction of the Gazi Atik Ali Pasha Mosque was started under the orders of the future Grand Vizier Hadım Atik Ali Pasha in 1496 and was completed in 1497, during the reign of Sultan Bayezid II.
The Gazi Atik Ali Pasha Mosque is located near the entrance to the Kapalıçarşı (Grand Bazaar), the Column of Constantine, and the historical Nuruosmaniye Mosque.
Atik Ali Pasha Mosque may refer to one of two mosques built in the Fatih district of Istanbul, Turkey, by the late 15th- and early 16th-century Ottoman statesman Hadım Atik Ali Pasha.

Hadım Atik Ali Pasha was a late 15th- and early 16th-century Ottoman statesman who had two mosques built in the Fatih district of Istanbul, Turkey, both of which are referred to by the name Atik Ali Pasha Mosque.

The Pertevniyal Valide Sultan Mosque, also known as the Aksaray Valide Mosque, is an Ottoman imperial mosque in Istanbul, Turkey, located at the intersection of Ordu Street and Atatürk Boulevard in the Aksaray neighborhood.
The Pertevniyal Valide Sultan Mosque is located next to Pertevniyal High School, which was also built by order of Sultana Pertevniyal in 1872.
Atik Mustafa Pasha Mosque, also named Hazreti Cabir Camii, is a former Eastern Orthodox church in Istanbul that was converted into a mosque by the Ottomans.

The dedication of the church that became the Atik Mustafa Pasha Mosque is obscure; for a long time it was identified with the church of Saints Peter and Mark without any proof, but it now seems more probable that it is the church of Saint Thekla of the Palace of Blachernae.
The building of the Atik Mustafa Pasha Mosque, a former church, belongs stylistically to the eleventh-twelfth century.

The Vasat Atik Ali Pasha Mosque, also known as Zincirlikuyu Mosque or Karagümrük Mosque, is an Ottoman mosque located in the Karagümrük neighbourhood of the Fatih district in Istanbul, Turkey, on Fevzipaşa Street.

Sultan Bayezid II's grand vizier Hadım Atik Ali Pasha, after whom the Vasat Atik Ali Pasha Mosque is named, ordered its construction in 1502, and it was completed in 1512, one year after the grand vizier's death.

The Valens Aqueduct, known in Turkish as Valens Su Kemeri or Bozdoğan Kemeri, meaning 'Aqueduct of the Grey Falcon', is a Roman aqueduct that was the major water-providing system of the Eastern Roman capital of Constantinople, modern Istanbul, Turkey.
The Valens Aqueduct was completed by Roman Emperor Valens in the late 4th century AD, and it was maintained and used by the Byzantines and later the Ottomans.
The Valens Aqueduct remains one of the most important landmarks of Istanbul, and its Ancient Greek name was Agogos tou hydatos, meaning simply 'aqueduct'.
The Atik Valide Mosque, Turkish Atik Valide Camii or Eski Valide Camii, is an Ottoman mosque located on the hill above a large and densely populated district of Üsküdar in Istanbul, Turkey.
The Atik Valide Mosque is an Ottoman mosque in Üsküdar, Istanbul, Turkey, and its Turkish names include Atik Valide Camii and Eski Valide Camii.
The Šarena džamija (colourful mosque), formally the Atik Behram Bey mosque, is the oldest mosque in Tuzla, Bosnia and Herzegovina.
The Šarena džamija, a name meaning colourful mosque, refers to the Atik Behram Bey mosque in Tuzla, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Alice Russell Glenny (1858-1924) was an American painter, sculptor, and graphic artist who lived and worked in Buffalo, New York, and was a fixture of the city's thriving artistic scene in the early twentieth century.
Alice Russell Glenny served as president of the Buffalo Society of Artists from 1893-1894 and again from 1903-1904.
Alice Russell Glenny studied under top teachers William Merritt Chase and Gustav Boulanger in both the United States and France, and was considered in her time to be one of Buffalo's top artists.
Alice Russell Glenny is best remembered today for her Art Nouveau posters and magazine illustrations, and her posters were featured prominently at Buffalo's Pan-American Exposition of 1901.
Alice Russell Glenny regularly contributed illustrations to the Buffalo-Courier Express, one of the major newspapers in Buffalo at the time.

James A. Garfield, the 20th President of the United States, was assassinated at 9:30 am on July 2, 1881, less than four months into his term, when Charles J. Guiteau shot him at the Baltimore and Potomac Railroad Station in Washington, D.C.
James A. Garfield died in Elberon, New Jersey on September 19, 1881, and his assassin Charles J. Guiteau was motivated by revenge against James A. Garfield for an imagined political debt.
James A. Garfield was the second of four Presidents to be assassinated, following Abraham Lincoln and preceding William McKinley and John F. Kennedy.
After James A. Garfield's death, his Vice President, Chester A. Arthur, succeeded him as President.

Rosalie Compton Kahipuleokalaniahumanu Davison, known as Rose C. Davison (September 22, 1868 to May 26, 1913), was a part Native Hawaiian female educator, philanthropist and governmental social worker.
Rose C. Davison served as assistant secretary of the Board of Education of the Territory of Hawaii and represented Hawaii at the 1901 Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo, New York.
Mission furniture is a style of furniture that originated in the late 19th century, tracing its origins to a chair made by A.J. Forbes around 1894 for San Francisco's Swedenborgian Church.

The term mission furniture was first popularized by Joseph P. McHugh of New York, a furniture manufacturer and retailer who copied these chairs and offered a line of stylistically related furnishings by 1898.

The word 'mission' in mission furniture references the Spanish missions throughout colonial California, though the design of most mission furniture owed little to the original furnishings of these missions.
Mission furniture became increasingly popular following the 1901 Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo and was popularly associated with the American Arts and Crafts movement.
The Pan-American Exposition was a World's Fair held in Buffalo, New York, United States, from May 1 through November 2, 1901.
The Pan-American Exposition occupied 350 acres of land on the western edge of what is now Delaware Park, extending from Delaware Avenue to Elmwood Avenue and northward to Great Arrow Avenue.
The Pan-American Exposition is remembered today primarily as the location of the assassination of President William McKinley.
Caroline Peddle Ball (1869-1938) was an American sculptor who was born at Terre Haute, Indiana, and was a pupil at the Art Students' League under Augustus Saint-Gaudens and Kenyon Cox.
Caroline Peddle Ball received honorable mention at the Paris Exhibition of 1900, was a member of the Guild of Arts and Crafts and of the Art Students' League, and exhibited a Bronze Clock at Paris.
Caroline Peddle Ball designed the figure of the Young Virgin and that of the Christ of the Sacred Heart for the Tiffany Glass Company.

Caroline Peddle Ball's important works include a memorial fountain at Flushing, Long Island, a medallion portrait of Miss Cox of Terre Haute, a monument to a child in Terre Haute, and a Victory in a quadriga seen on the United States Building in Paris in 1900 and at the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo in 1901.
The Temple of Music was a concert hall and auditorium built for the Pan-American Exposition held in Buffalo, New York in 1901.
U.S. President William McKinley was assassinated inside the Temple of Music on September 6, 1901.
Like most of the other buildings at the Pan-American Exposition, the Temple of Music was demolished when the fair ended.

The 1901 State of the Union Address was given on Tuesday, December 3, 1901, by the 26th President of the United States, Theodore Roosevelt, and was presented to both houses of the 57th United States Congress, though Theodore Roosevelt was not present.

In the 1901 State of the Union Address, Theodore Roosevelt stated that Congress assembled that year under the shadow of a great calamity: President McKinley was shot by an anarchist while attending the Pan-American Exposition at Buffalo on September 6 and died in that city on September 14.

In the 1901 State of the Union Address, Theodore Roosevelt said the nation was at peace with the nations of mankind and that the country firmly intended its policy to continue unbroken, maintaining international relations of mutual respect and good will.
'Put Me Off at Buffalo' is a song by the vaudeville team of the Dillon Brothers, with lyrics by Harry Dillon and music by John Dillon, first published in 1895.

'Put Me Off at Buffalo' also appeared in the play 'A Trip to Chinatown', and after an initial period of popularity the tune was revived in 1901 in connection with the Pan-American Exposition held in Buffalo.
During the 1901 Pan-American Exposition, the lyrics of 'Put Me Off at Buffalo' were planted in the lawn of Buffalo's city hall.
On September 6, 1901, William McKinley, the 25th President of the United States, was shot on the grounds of the Pan-American Exposition at the Temple of Music in Buffalo, New York.
William McKinley was shaking hands with the public when Leon Czolgosz, an anarchist, shot him twice in the abdomen.

William McKinley died eight days later, on September 14, of gangrene caused by the gunshot wounds, and he was the third American president to have been assassinated, following Abraham Lincoln in 1865 and James A. Garfield in 1881.
